what_its_for: Insulin glargine-aglr is a long-acting insulin used to help control blood sugar levels in adults and children (6 years and older) with type 1 diabetes, and in adults with type 2 diabetes. It works by replacing or supplementing the insulin your body normally makes to keep your blood sugar in a healthy range.
how_to_take: This insulin is given as a shot (injection) under the skin (subcutaneous injection) — NOT into a vein or muscle. You can inject it in your stomach area (abdomen), upper thigh, or upper arm. Rotate your injection sites each time to avoid skin problems. Always use a new needle for each injection. Do not shake the pen — roll it gently between your palms if needed. Check the insulin before each use: it should look clear and colorless. Do not use it if it looks cloudy, colored, or has particles in it.
dosing: Your dose is decided by your doctor based on your blood sugar levels, diet, activity level, and other factors — there is no standard one-size-fits-all dose. This insulin is typically injected ONCE a day, at the SAME time every day. Do not change your dose unless your doctor tells you to. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, check your blood sugar and contact your doctor or diabetes care team right away for guidance on what to do next. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. After a missed dose, get back on your regular once-daily schedule as directed by your doctor.
storage: Store unopened (unused) pens in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze. Do not use insulin that has been frozen. Keep away from direct heat and light. Once you start using a pen (in-use pen), you may store it at room temperature (below 86°F / 30°C) for up to 28 days — do NOT put it back in the refrigerator. Always put the cap back on the pen when not in use. Keep out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol, as it can cause unpredictable changes in your blood sugar — either too high or too low. Do not skip meals after taking your insulin. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel symptoms of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Do not mix this insulin with any other insulin or liquid in the same syringe. Avoid injecting into the same spot every time to prevent hard lumps or pits in the skin. Do not share your insulin pen or needles with anyone else — this can spread serious infections.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you have signs of LOW blood sugar (hypoglycemia): shakiness, sweating, fast heartbeat, dizziness, confusion, headache, blurred vision, or fainting. Call your doctor if you have signs of HIGH blood sugar (hyperglycemia): increased thirst, frequent urination, blurry vision, or fruity-smelling breath. Also contact your doctor if you notice skin reactions at your injection site (redness, swelling, itching, or thickening), signs of an allergic reaction (rash, shortness of breath, swelling of face or throat), low potassium levels (muscle weakness or cramps), or if you are sick, stressed, or have a change in diet or activity that may affect your blood sugar.
when_it_works: Insulin glargine-aglr is a long-acting insulin. It starts working within 1 to 2 hours after injection and provides a steady, even level of insulin over about 24 hours — with no sharp peaks. It is designed to control your background (basal) blood sugar throughout the day and night. You may not feel it working, but it is helping keep your blood sugar stable around the clock. It may take several days of consistent use and dose adjustments by your doctor before your blood sugar is well controlled.
special_populations: Children: This medication can be used in children 6 years and older with type 1 diabetes. Dosing is determined by a doctor. Older adults (65+): Older adults may be more sensitive to insulin and have a higher risk of low blood sugar. Blood sugar should be monitored closely. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Insulin needs often change during pregnancy and after delivery. Your doctor will monitor and adjust your dose carefully. Kidney or liver disease: Your insulin dose may need to be adjusted if you have kidney or liver problems, as these conditions can affect how your body processes insulin. Always tell your doctor about all your medical conditions and medications.
